openingProblem.problem: West Germany became a democracy after total defeat and occupation; Spain after a dictator's death; Argentina after a lost war; South Africa after decades of resistance and four years of negotiation. Is there a common recipe for democracy, or does each state make its own?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: what do all four transitions have in common?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Why did democracy emerge? Four sets of conditions
chunks.body:
Topic 9 asks you to explain the **conditions** in which democratic states emerged. The four states in this course show four different routes.

In **West Germany**, democracy followed total defeat. After the unconditional surrender of May 1945, sovereignty passed to the Allies, who supervised the drafting of the Basic Law. Mary Fulbrook argues that the division that produced a separate West German state was "an ad hoc unintended result of the emerging Cold War". Democracy here was shaped by outside powers.

In **Spain** and **Argentina**, democracy followed the end of a dictatorship, but in very different ways. In Spain the dictator died in office in November 1975, and the transition was managed from inside the regime. In Argentina, the military regime that seized power in March 1976 collapsed after its defeat in the Falklands war of 1982 and handed over power to an elected president in December 1983.

In **South Africa**, democracy had to be won for the majority from a minority government that had denied it to them since 1948. Historians disagree about the decisive pressure: Chris Saunders stresses the mass uprising of the 1980s, while Nigel Worden sees the fall of the Berlin Wall as critical to the timing of De Klerk's announcement in February 1990. Francis Wilson argues that the end of the Cold War "facilitated" change but "did not cause it".

Comparing these routes shows a pattern: democracy emerged when the old order lost its legitimacy, through military defeat (Germany, Argentina), the death of a dictator in a changed society (Spain), or mass resistance combined with international isolation (South Africa).

This mattered because the way democracy emerged shaped what it had to deal with, which meant that each new democracy inherited different problems: occupation, impunity, an unreformed state, or deep inequality.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Defeat produced democracy in Germany and Argentina.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Germany was occupied; Argentina was not.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Spain's transition came from inside the regime.
South Africa's change came from pressure and negotiation.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Historians disagree on the decisive factor.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Military defeat created the conditions for democracy in both Germany and Argentina, but in different ways.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Germany surrendered unconditionally in May 1945 and lost its sovereignty to the Allies, whereas Argentina's junta fell into disrepute after the Falklands defeat of 1982 but kept control until handing power to Alfonsín in December 1983.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that German democracy was designed under Allied supervision, while Argentine democracy was built by Argentines who had to deal with a military that was still intact.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, in both cases defeat discredited the old rulers, which removed the main obstacle to democracy.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Defeat was therefore a common cause, but occupation made Germany's emergence more controlled than Argentina's.

chunks.title: Who made the transition? Negotiation, imposition and collapse
chunks.body:
Transitions can be compared by asking **who made them**.

**Spain** is the clearest case of a transition from above. Adolfo Suárez, a former Francoist official, persuaded the Francoist assembly to vote for reform, which passed by referendum on 15 December 1976 with over 94 per cent. Tony Judt argues that democracy was made "by conservative statesmen from the old regime itself". But once elections were held, consensus with the left and unions, in the Moncloa Pacts and the 1978 Constitution, completed it.

**South Africa** was a negotiated transition between enemies. De Klerk's announcement of 2 February 1990 opened four years of talks with the ANC. The breakthrough was the Record of Understanding of 1992, with Joe Slovo's "sunset clauses" guaranteeing power-sharing for five years. The result was the election of April 1994.

**West Germany** was a supervised transition: German politicians drafted the Basic Law, but under close Allied monitoring.

**Argentina** was a transition by collapse: the discredited junta called elections and handed over power to Alfonsín, who won 51.75 per cent in October 1983. There was no negotiated pact with the military, which later forced the Law of Due Obedience on the new democracy.

Each route had a price. Negotiation required concessions to the old rulers (South Africa's sunset clauses, Spain's continuity of personnel). Collapse left the old rulers intact and resentful (Argentina). Supervision limited sovereignty (Germany).

This mattered because the terms of the transition decided how far the new democracy could deal with the old regime, which meant that negotiated transitions bought stability at the cost of justice.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Spain's transition was made from above.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The left completed it by consensus.

argumentsThatWork.claim: South Africa's transition was negotiated between enemies.

useItInAnEssay.judge: Both transitions therefore succeeded because the old rulers were reassured, though South Africa's change of power was far greater.

chunks.title: Dealing with the past: truth, trials, amnesty and silence
chunks.body:
Every new democracy had to decide what to do about the crimes of the regime before it. The four states made four different choices.

**Argentina** went furthest at first. CONADEP listed 8,960 disappeared people, and in December 1985 the Trial of the Juntas sentenced Videla and Massera to life imprisonment. But under military pressure the Law of Due Obedience of 1987 protected most officers, and in 1989–90 Menem pardoned the junta leaders.

**South Africa** chose **restorative justice**. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission heard more than 22,000 victims in 1996–98 and granted amnesty to perpetrators who made a full disclosure; only 1,167 of 7,116 applications succeeded.

**West Germany** at first avoided its past. In 1949 the Federal Republic ended investigations into the Nazi past of civil servants, and in 1951 most Bavarian judges were ex-Nazis. Only with the Eichmann trial of 1961 and the Frankfurt Auschwitz trials of 1963–65 did Nazi crimes come to wide public attention.

**Spain** chose silence. Judt notes the absence of any reference to the recent past in post-transition Spain, and democratic governments themselves committed abuses: the GAL killed twenty-six ETA members in 1983–87.

Comparing them shows a dilemma. Trials, as in Argentina, risked provoking the military; amnesty or silence, as in Spain and early West Germany, bought stability but left injustice; South Africa's TRC tried to find a path between them, offering truth in exchange for amnesty.

This mattered because how a democracy dealt with the past affected its legitimacy, which meant that justice, truth and stability had to be balanced differently in each state.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The junta leaders were convicted first.

argumentsThatWork.claim: South Africa chose truth and amnesty.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Many victims felt justice was denied.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Germany and Spain at first avoided the past.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Germany later held the Auschwitz trials.

chunks.title: Consolidating democracy: constitutions, alternation and economic policy
chunks.body:
A democracy is often called **consolidated** when its rules are accepted by all major forces and power changes hands peacefully. The four states reached this point by different paths.

**Constitutions** were central. West Germany's Basic Law of 1949 corrected Weimar's weaknesses with a constructive vote of no confidence and allowed anti-democratic parties to be banned. Spain's 1978 Constitution created a parliamentary monarchy with regional autonomy. South Africa's 1996 constitution created a Bill of Rights and a Constitutional Court. Argentina's 1994 reform declared any break in constitutional order illegal.

**Alternation in power** was the test. West Germany passed it in 1969, when the SPD took office. Spain passed it in 1982 and again in 1996, when the Socialists lost to the People's Party. Argentina passed it in 1989 and in 1999, when de la Rúa defeated the Peronists. South Africa, where the ANC won 66.36 per cent in 1999, had not yet passed it: Thompson calls it a "one-party democracy", though with strong checks.

**Economic policy** shaped public support. West Germany's social market economy doubled GNP by 1955. Spain's Moncloa Pacts eased the economic crisis of the transition, and EC entry in 1986 anchored Spain in Europe. Menem's Convertibility ended Argentina's hyperinflation, but privatisation pushed unemployment above 10 per cent; South Africa's GEAR shifted policy towards growth, but the Gini index of inequality rose.

This mattered because democracy proved most secure where prosperity and peaceful alternation went together, which meant that West Germany and Spain consolidated faster than Argentina and South Africa.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Rules alone did not guarantee stability.
South Africa had no change of governing party by 2000.
Unemployment and inequality remained in Argentina and South Africa.

howItGetsAsked: Analyse the role of constitutions in consolidating democracy in two states, each chosen from a different region, between 1949 and 1996.
Evaluate the success of economic policies in two democratic states between 1949 and 1999.

useItInAnEssay.claim: West Germany and South Africa both used constitutions to protect democracy, but they faced different threats.
useItInAnEssay.prove: West Germany's Basic Law introduced the constructive vote of no confidence against Weimar-style instability, whereas South Africa's 1996 constitution created a Bill of Rights and a Constitutional Court to protect rights after apartheid.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the Basic Law was designed above all for stable government, while South Africa's constitution was designed above all for equal rights.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, both relied on more than rules: West Germany on prosperity and South Africa on checks such as a free press and civil society.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Constitutions were therefore necessary in both, but their design reflected the failures each state was trying to avoid.

historiography.useItLikeThis: Judt's view supports the claim that transitions from above can succeed, which suggests a useful contrast with South Africa, where change was negotiated between the regime and its excluded majority.

misconceptions.right: They followed **four routes**: occupation, reform from above, collapse, and negotiation.

misconceptions.wrong: A new constitution is enough to consolidate democracy.
misconceptions.right: Consolidation also needs **peaceful alternation** and public support, often through prosperity.

segments.text: Negotiation with the old regime made transitions smoother, but it was not the only route to democracy.
Spain's reform referendum of December 1976 and the Moncloa Pacts reassured the old regime, whereas Argentina's junta simply collapsed and handed power to Alfonsín in 1983.
This meant that Spain's army largely accepted democracy after 1981, while Argentina's resentful military forced the Due Obedience law in 1987.
However, Argentina's democracy also survived, alternating power peacefully in 1989 and 1999.
The claim is therefore valid for the stability of transitions, but overstated as a condition of success.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the reasons for, and the results of, the ways in which two democratic states dealt with the crimes of previous regimes between 1945 and 1999.
essayQuestions.scope: Argentina and South Africa (or any two of the four states)

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.factorOrTask: Two tasks: reasons AND results, in two states
decodeKey.judgement: Which approach produced more truth, justice and stability?

modelPlan.thesis: Argentina chose trials because its military had been discredited, but revolts forced a retreat into amnesty and pardons; South Africa chose truth for amnesty because its transition was negotiated, which produced more truth and less conflict.
modelPlan.counter: In both, most perpetrators were never punished.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which result mattered most? South Africa gained more truth with less conflict.

segments.text: Argentina and South Africa dealt with the past differently because their transitions were different.

Argentina's junta had collapsed after the Falklands, so Alfonsín could put it on trial, whereas South Africa's negotiated settlement required amnesty, offered by the TRC in exchange for full disclosure.
This meant that Argentina sentenced Videla and Massera to life in 1985 but provoked military revolts, while South Africa's TRC heard over 22,000 victims without such a backlash.
However, Argentina's Due Obedience law and Menem's pardons left most perpetrators free, much as amnesty did in South Africa.
The results were therefore similar for punishment, but South Africa's approach produced more truth and stability.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the success of economic policies in two democratic states between 1949 and 1999.
essayQuestions.scope: West Germany and Argentina (or any two of the four states)

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge

modelPlan.thesis: West Germany's social market economy was the more successful, combining growth with social security and so strengthening democracy; Argentina's Convertibility ended hyperinflation but raised unemployment and debt.

arguments.claim: West Germany: the social market economy.
Comparison: inequality (South Africa as a further case).

modelPlan.counter: Both policies brought stability after economic disaster: post-war collapse in Germany, hyperinflation in Argentina.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Success by what criterion? Growth with social security: Germany; stability alone: both.

segments.text: West Germany's economic policy was more successful than Argentina's, because it combined growth with social security.
Erhard's social market economy doubled GNP by 1955, whereas Menem's Convertibility of 1991 ended hyperinflation but was followed by privatisation and rising unemployment.
This meant that West Germans associated democracy with prosperity, while in Argentina unemployment and corruption helped defeat the Peronists in 1999.
However, both policies succeeded in their first aim, stabilising an economy after disaster.
West Germany's policy was therefore more successful because its social side spread the benefits of growth.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the role of constitutions in consolidating democracy in two states, each chosen from a different region, between 1949 and 1996.
essayQuestions.scope: West Germany and South Africa (or any two of the four states from different regions)

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: How far did the rules secure democracy?

modelPlan.thesis: Constitutions were designed against each state's past failures, the Basic Law against Weimar's instability and South Africa's 1996 constitution against apartheid's denial of rights; both secured democracy only together with peaceful politics and social support.
modelPlan.counter: South Africa had no change of governing party by 2000 despite its constitution.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which constitution did more? The Basic Law, because it worked with alternation in 1969.

segments.text: Both constitutions were designed against the failures of the past, but they protected democracy in different ways.
The Basic Law introduced the constructive vote of no confidence, whereas South Africa's 1996 constitution created a Bill of Rights and a Constitutional Court that abolished the death penalty.
This meant that West Germany's constitution secured stable government, while South Africa's secured individual rights against the state.
However, West Germany saw a peaceful change of government in 1969, whereas South Africa's ANC won 66.36 per cent in 1999, which Thompson calls a 'one-party democracy'.
Constitutions were therefore essential in both, but consolidation also depended on alternation, which only West Germany achieved within the period.
